source_metadata.title: Cutaneous adverse drug reactions: An 8-year retrospective study on hospitalized patients in Southern China
source_metadata.journal: Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology, and Leprology
source_metadata.source_type: Letter to the Editor; retrospective hospital-based study

atoms.canonical_statement: The study aimed to assess recent trends in clinical types of cutaneous adverse drug reactions (CADRs) and their causative agents over 8 years in a hospital-based population in Southern China.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The purpose of this study was to assess recent trends of clinical types of CADRs and their causative agents in a hospital-based population for a period of 8 years in Southern China.

atoms.canonical_statement: The investigators retrospectively analyzed clinical data for inpatients diagnosed with CADR from January 2003 through December 2010.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The clinical data of inpatients, diagnosed with CADR in our hospital from January 2003 to December 2010, were retrospectively analyzed.

atoms.canonical_statement: All reactions were reviewed by dermatologists and diagnosed according to the WHO definition of CADR.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: All reactions were reviewed by dermatologists and diagnosed in accordance with the definition of CADR provided by WHO.

atoms.canonical_statement: Severe CADRs were defined as exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, or drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms; all other CADRs were classified as non-severe.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Exfoliative dermatitis (ED), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) were classified as severe (S)-CADRs, and other cases with CADRs that did not fall into the S-CADRs category were termed non-severe (NS)-CADRs.

atoms.canonical_statement: Dermatology-department data from 2003-2010 were compared with a previous same-ward study of 198 CADR cases from May 1984 to May 1994.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Data collected from inpatients of dermatological department were compared to those in a previous study, involving 198 CADRs cases from the same ward in the period from May 1984 to May 1994.

atoms.canonical_statement: Statistical analyses used Stata 10.0; differences in CADR prevalence were assessed with Fisher exact probability tests and P<0.05 was treated as significant.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: All statistical tests were performed with software Stata 10.0. Differences in prevalence of CADRs were assessed by Fisher exact probability test. Correlations were regarded as significant when P < 0.05.

atoms.canonical_statement: During 2003-2010, 524 CADR cases were identified among 364,636 hospitalized patients, corresponding to a reported prevalence of 1.4 per 1000 hospitalizations.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: During the 8-year period, a total of 524 patients were diagnosed with CADRs among 364,636 hospitalized patients. The prevalence of CADRs among hospitalized patients was 1.4/1000.

atoms.canonical_statement: For traditional Chinese medicine-associated CADRs, the causative ingredient was difficult to identify because of the complex composition.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: However, due to the complex composition, the causative ingredient of TCM was difficult to identify.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors suggested that higher cephalosporin- and fluoroquinolone-associated CADR percentages might reflect increased exposure to those antibiotics, while lower sulfonamide-associated CADRs might reflect decreased sulfonamide use.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The high incidences of cephalosporins-induced CADRs and fluoroquinolones-induced CARDs may be associated with increased exposure to cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones in certain populations because of florid usage of those antibiotics. The decline in use of sulfonamides in recent years could result in the low incidence of sulfonamides-induced CARDs.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors suggested that increased use of allopurinol and carbamazepine could explain increased EM-like eruptions and severe CADRs, especially SJS and TEN.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The increased administration of allopurinol and cabamazepine in recent years could be the reason for the increased incidences of EM-like eruptions and S-CADRs, especially SJS and TEN.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors suggested that lower hospitalization of patients with exanthematous reactions and fixed drug eruptions might explain the lower prevalence of these clinical types compared with the historical study.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The prevalences of ER or FDE in hospitalized patients were decreased compared to that of the previous study. The reason might be that more patients with ER and FDE were not hospitalized in recent years.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that CADRs should not be overlooked in hospital settings and reported increased proportions attributed to allopurinol, carbamazepine, cephalosporins, and traditional Chinese medicine, with higher proportions of EM-like eruptions, SJS, and TEN.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Briefly, our study emphasized that CADR couldn’t be overlooked in a hospital environment. Percentages of CADRs caused by allopurinol, carbamazepine, cephalosporins, and TCM were increased. Higher percentages of EM-like eruptions, SJS and TEN were also seen.
